definition: A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant every other token is when computing a representation of the current token.
details: In the Transformer, each token produces a query, key and value vector; attention scores are the dot products of queries with keys, scaled and normalized with a softmax, then used to blend the values. Multi-head attention runs this several times in parallel so the model can attend to different relationships at once. It is the core of modern LLMs such as GPT and BERT.
story: Think of an orchestra warming up: no single instrument carries the piece, but together they make the sound. At the bottom of every machine is a design — the shape of it, and how its pieces talk to each other. The layout decides what the machine can even attempt, before it learns a single thing. The shape of the machine is half the idea. And that shape of the machine — Attention — is what makes everything else possible.

citation.title: Attention Is All You Need
citation.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NeurIPS)

explainer.lead: Attention lets a model decide, for every word it is reading, which other words matter most right now.
explainer.eli5: When you read "the cat sat because it was tired", you know "it" means the cat. Attention gives a model the same trick: for each word it looks back at all the other words and pays the most attention to the ones that help it understand.
explainer.practitioner: Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. Scores are dot products between one token's query and every key, softmaxed into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of values. In practice you use multi-head scaled dot-product attention (e.g. torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention), add a causal mask for decoders, and watch the quadratic memory cost in sequence length — FlashAttention, KV caching and sliding windows are the usual mitigations.
explainer.paperLevel: Scaled dot-product attention computes Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V, where the √d_k factor keeps logits from saturating the softmax as dimension grows. Multi-head attention runs h such maps on learned projections and concatenates them. It generalises the additive alignment model of Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2014) and is the sole sequence-mixing operation in the Transformer of Vaswani et al. (2017); its O(n²) time and memory in sequence length motivates sparse, linear and IO-aware variants.
explainer.intuition: Instead of squeezing a whole sentence into one fixed summary, the model keeps every word available and, at each step, looks up the parts that are relevant — like skimming back through notes for the line you need.
howItWorks: Turn each token into three vectors: a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain?) and a value (what do I pass on?).
Score the query against every key with a dot product and divide by the square root of the key size.
Softmax the scores so they become weights that sum to one.
Blend the value vectors with those weights to get the token's new, context-aware representation.
Repeat in several heads in parallel so different heads can track different relationships.
explainer.example: Translating "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired", the attention weights for "it" peak on "animal"; change "tired" to "wide" and they shift toward "street".
explainer.whyItMatters: Attention removed the bottleneck of recurrent encoders and parallelises across the whole sequence, which is what made training today's large language models practical.
misconceptions: Attention weights are not a faithful explanation of a model's reasoning; they show where information flowed, not why.
Attention is not only for text — the same operation powers vision transformers, speech models and protein models.
